drapeaux.note: The two short quotations in the body (the line from Le Pédant joué, and Le Bret's phrase about Cyrano's reserve toward women) are French originals; no published English rendering was found, so they are translated faithfully from the French.

The French says Le Bret's preface was published “twenty months after his death in 1657,” which reads as if Cyrano died in 1657 (he died in 1655; the preface is from 1657). Translated as “published in 1657, twenty months after his death” to avoid the wrong reading; the French wording should be clarified.

titre: Cyrano de Bergerac was not a Gascon
accroche: The real Cyrano de Bergerac was a Parisian, not a Gascon, and his love letters, found after his death, were addressed to men.
contenu_vulgarise:
The panache, the accent of the Southwest, the duel improvised in verse: Edmond Rostand's play fixed, in 1897, an image of Cyrano so vivid that it erased the real man. Yet the latter is nothing like a Gascon cadet. Savinien de Cyrano de Bergerac was born in Paris in 1619, on the rue des Deux-Portes, into a family of bourgeois enriched by financial speculation, a family that had simply bought, in the Chevreuse valley, lands called Bergerac. Nothing Gascon in that.

## Where the Confusion Still Comes From

At twenty, Cyrano enlists in the musketeer company of Carbon de Casteljaloux, a company made up overwhelmingly of Gascons, which is enough to make people believe, afterward, that he was one himself. His military experience is cut short: two serious wounds, a musket shot to the body and then a sword thrust to the throat during the sieges of Mouzon and Arras, push him to quit. Back in Paris, he settles into libertine and learned circles, frequents the philosopher Gassendi, and writes pamphlets during the Fronde, a tragedy that causes a scandal (*La Mort d'Agrippine* (*The Death of Agrippina*), 1654) and a comedy, *Le Pédant joué* (*The Pedant Tricked*), which leaves posterity a line that Molière later takes up: “What was he doing in that galley?”

## What the First Biographer Keeps Quiet

Most of what we know about Cyrano comes from a preface written by his friend Henry Le Bret, published in 1657, twenty months after his death. Le Bret is also a man of the cloth, and his text, frankly hagiographic, lends the libertine atheist a final conversion that historians find hardly credible, and passes over in silence a fact that Cyrano's letters nonetheless make visible: he preferred men, and published his love letters while pretending they were addressed to women. Le Bret contents himself with mentioning, cautiously, his “great restraint toward the fair sex.”

## What This Shifts

The Cyrano everyone knows is thus a fiction built on another fiction. Le Bret, in 1657, is already smoothing away what was troubling in his friend's life in order to make a presentable portrait. Two and a half centuries later, Rostand adds his own layer: an outsized nose, a Gascon origin, and above all an unhappy love for Roxane that fills the entire play, whereas nothing in the sources indicates that the real Cyrano loved women. Each generation has not simply embellished the real man: it has redrawn, to its own measure, what it judged tellable about him.

repere.texte: Cyrano is not Gascon at all: born in Paris, he enlists at twenty in a musketeer company made up mostly of Gascons, which is why he was believed to be one.
repere.source: Christine Genin, Gallica blog — Bibliothèque nationale de France, 2019

carte.punch: Cyrano de Bergerac was not a Gascon: he was born in Paris, and he preferred men.
carte.idee: The real Cyrano de Bergerac, born in Paris in 1619, was not a Gascon: his bourgeois family had simply bought lands called Bergerac. His first biographer kept quiet about his preference for men; Rostand, in 1897, added the nose, the Gascon origin and the love for Roxane.

quiz.question: What does Henry Le Bret, Cyrano's first biographer and friend, do in the preface he publishes in 1657?
choix: He reveals for the first time Cyrano's homosexuality, until then kept secret
He invents out of whole cloth the existence of the Cadets of Gascony to dramatize the story
He keeps quiet about Cyrano's preference for men, and lends him a dubious final religious conversion
He publishes the complete manuscripts of Cyrano without any modification
quiz.explication: Le Bret, a loyal friend but also a man of the cloth, writes a hagiographic preface: he keeps quiet about Cyrano's preference for men behind a cautious phrase and attributes to him a final conversion that historians find hardly credible. It is neither a revelation, nor the invention of the Cadets of Gascony, which came later and is Rostand's doing, nor a complete edition: the first posthumous editions are heavily reworked.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which line from Cyrano's Le Pédant joué (The Pedant Tricked) is later taken up by Molière?
choix: The best is the enemy of the good
What was he doing in that galley?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Le Pédant joué leaves posterity the line “What was he doing in that galley?”, later taken up by Molière in one of his own plays.

quiz_supplementaire.question: During which sieges is Cyrano gravely wounded, before leaving the army?
choix: The sieges of Mouzon and Arras
The sieges of La Rochelle and Montauban
The sieges of Paris and Orléans
The sieges of Metz and Verdun
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Cyrano receives a musket shot to the body and then a sword thrust to the throat during the sieges of Mouzon and Arras, which pushes him to give up his military enlistment.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does the name Bergerac, borne by Cyrano's family, come from?
choix: From a noble title bought from the crown
From a town in Périgord where the family owned a château
From lands bought in the Chevreuse valley, called Bergerac
From a Gascon ancestor originally from the town of Bergerac
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Cyrano's family, bourgeois enriched by financial speculation, had simply bought lands called Bergerac in the Chevreuse valley, with no connection to Gascony.
